transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Recording link: (shared) https://redwood.share/af/poc-ttft-2026-05-19
Notes: deck + benchmark sheet referenced in chat

Attendees:
- Jordan Klein (Redwood, AE)
- Priya Nair (Redwood, SE)
- Sam Torres (Redwood, CSM)
- Anita Rao (Redwood, SRE)
- Mike Patel (AcmeFinance, Eng Lead)
- Rita Gomez (AcmeFinance, ML Infra)
- David Chen (AcmeFinance, Benchmarks)
- Hannah Li (AcmeFinance, Security)
- Tom (AcmeFinance, Product)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining today. quick agenda — priya will walk through the latest TTFT traces, we'll go over streaming behavior, sequence length mix, kernel choices and next steps. any blockers before we start?

[00:28] Mike: no blockers, just curious if we can get TTFT under 120ms for our chat path. current baseline is around 210 with our client setup.

[00:35] Priya: ok great, that's what we focused on this week. quick reminder — we ran three configs: hosted default (streaming off), hosted with streaming on, and dedicated 4-gpu pool with kernel override + quantization profile Q4_0. I put the raw traces in the benchmark sheet. link in chat.

[01:05] David: small caveat — our test harness sends synthetic traffic at median seq len 96 tokens, but production has 30-40 tokens median. earlier runs inflated tail numbers.

[01:22] Priya: good call, we included a mix run with 32-token median; I'll call those the client-mix runs.

[01:34] [02:00] Priya: showing slide, hosted default — TTFT median 210ms, p95 380ms. streaming off so whole response is generated before first token. CPU overhead on gateway for request prep about 15-18ms. model served on g4dn-equivalent, not quantized.

[03:10] Priya: hosted + streaming — TTFT median dropped to 110ms, p95 270ms. this was with streaming enabled and kernel path default. key win: removing the pipeline wait for full response cut the TTFT in half. however we saw an increase in token-to-token jitter for long streams.

[04:12] Rita: can you clarify "kernel path default" — is that automatic selection by runtime?

[04:21] Priya: yes runtime picks kernels based on model arch and seq length heuristics; for these runs it selected aten kernels on the GPU. when we forced optimized attention kernels in the dedicated run we saw latency improvement for short sequences.

[05:00] Anita: for dedicated we did kernel override + Q4_0 quantization, right? any perf regressions on quality?

[05:07] Priya: we ran internal evals — slight drop in perplexity but for our task (instruction-following chat) quality delta was negligible. customer should run their evals.

[05:40] [06:00] Priya: dedicated 4-GPU pool with optimized kernels and caching enabled — TTFT median 85ms, p95 160ms. token streaming improves start but also KV cache warmup matters: for cold calls TTFT is dominated by model warmup and first KV populate.

[06:44] Mike: can you explain KV cache warmup? our clients open many short lived sessions.

[06:52] Priya: sure — if you start a new session the KV cache is empty and the runtime has to compute initial key/values for the first tokens, which adds overhead. Warm caching (prefix caching) or reusing sessions reduces that cost. also continuous batching heuristics can trade a few ms for throughput.

[07:35] Jordan: one practical lever is session pooling on the client side — keep sessions warm for short bursts. Mike, any constraints there?

[07:44] Mike: we can do short pooling, but our security team wants session isolation for certain flows — that may force cold starts.

[07:55] Hannah: correct — for some PII flows we need ephemeral sessions and audit logs; can't reuse session tokens across users. this will affect TTFT.

[08:12] Priya: noted — we can prioritize reducing cold-start TTFT. two things seemed promising: streaming + smaller models (or trimmed sequence length) and kernel choices tuned for short sequences.

[08:45] [09:00] Priya: diving deeper: sequence length impact — with median seq 32 TTFT median was 95ms hosted+streaming, with median 96 it was 110ms. so there is linear-ish growth. but more important is the first-token path: if you can shorten prompt prefix or offload heavy context embedding you get big wins.

[09:50] David: we run a heavy system prompt ~600 tokens plus 128 token user context in many flows. that's a problem.

[10:05] Tom: product needs the system prompt for safety filters. can we cache the system prompt embeddings on the server side?

[10:12] Priya: yes — Redwood supports prefix caching; you can precompute prefix KV and reuse across sessions. that reduces per-call compute. security team still needs to sign-off because it's persistent state.

[10:40] Hannah: as long as cached prefix is treated as ephemeral and encrypted at rest and we have audit logs, might be ok. what's the KMS flow?

[10:50] Anita: on dedicated/private we integrate with customer KMS; keys are customer-managed and audit logs are forwarded to their SIEM. we can add TTLs to cached prefixes.

[11:20] [12:00] Priya: next — kernel choices. On GPUs we tested default aten kernels vs fused attention kernels. For short sequences fused attention reduced per-token overhead and improved TTFT by ~10-20ms. For long sequences fused kernels did not help as much and sometimes increased jitter.

[12:50] Priya: also quantization profile matters: Q4_0 gave good latency and negligible quality drop; Q5 variants reduced memory but didn't change TTFT meaningfully.

[13:30] Mike: can we get per-kernel trace? i want to see where time is spent — kernel launch, memcpy, scheduling.

[13:38] Priya: yes we produced trace slices showing kernel launch and memcpy times; I'll upload per request. the redwood console trace view shows per-stage timings.

[14:10] Jordan: sharing a note — when streaming is on, the client must handle partial output and reassembly; our SDK has sample streaming client that handles buffering and reconnection. Luis can drop sample link.

[14:32] Luis: sample streaming SDK link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-streaming-sample

[14:40] [15:00] David: regarding networking — our infra adds 8-12ms egress+ingress; do you see that in your traces?

[15:08] Priya: yes traces include client-network. we separate out gateway processing (~15ms), network (~10ms median in our region), and model TTFT. so while model improvements help, client and gateway optimizations are also required to hit 120ms TTFT.

[15:40] Mike: what's realistic for production if we go dedicated with streaming + prefix cache?

[15:47] Priya: realistic median ~70-90ms for typical 32-token median and warmed prefix; cold starts may still be 140-180ms. with reserved burst capacity and session pooling you can achieve p95 in the ~120-150ms range for most flows.

[16:30] [17:00] Jordan: let's talk tradeoffs — dedicated costs more but gives lower TTFT and more kernel control; hosted is cheaper but you're limited on kernel overrides and KV cache policies. Mike, is budget a blocker?

[17:18] Mike: budget is flexible if it materially improves UX metrics. we need numbers to justify. please send cost/per-token and expected throughput.

[17:35] Jordan: will do — I'll send Dedicated vs Hosted cost model plus an example for 180M requests/month.

[18:00] Priya: next technical note — batching. continuous batching reduces per-token cost but can increase TTFT for isolated requests because the runtime waits a few ms to form batches. We tuned batching window to 4-6ms for this POC. If ultra-low TTFT is the goal we recommend small batching windows or disable for certain routes.

[18:42] Rita: what about dynamic batching based on route? we have mixed traffic.

[18:48] Priya: yes runtime supports route-level policies; the console can set SLO windows by route so critical flows get tighter batching.

[19:10] [20:00] Priya: showed a quick demo of streaming enabled in the SDK — client receives first token at about 95ms in the demo environment, reassembly works, reconnect fallback handled. There was a small transcript glitch in the demo due to client buffer threshold mismatch.

[20:38] Tom: will the SDK handle auth refresh seamlessly for streaming?

[20:45] Luis: yes sample handles token refresh; we recommend short-lived tokens with refresh flow to support ephemeral sessions.

[21:00] [22:00] Mike: security question — does prefix cache store unencrypted data?

[22:10] Anita: by default on hosted prefix cache is encrypted at rest; on Dedicated/Private we can integrate your KMS and ensure customer-managed keys. audit logs for cache access are available.

[22:40] Hannah: what retention and TTL controls do we have?

[22:50] Anita: TTLs are configurable per-prefix and can be as short as minutes; we can also evict on demand via API.

[23:20] [24:00] Priya: wanted to highlight an anomaly we saw: a small subset of requests showed TTFT spikes ~600ms. root cause was intermittent memcpy stalls when kernel scheduling overlapped with a background checkpoint on the node. On dedicated we can isolate workloads to avoid that.

[24:52] Priya: also, GPU driver versions impacted fused kernel perf; we matched drivers across nodes in the dedicated run.

[25:30] David: can you reproduce the spike consistently?

[25:35] Priya: we could reproduce under synthetic burst loads; under steady-state it's rare. Anita suggests isolated node pools for critical routes.

[26:10] Anita: yes isolate critical workloads to dedicated nodes. also enable node-level tracing to catch memcpy stalls early.

[26:40] [27:00] Jordan: let's align on immediate next steps and owners. Priya — can you run a 1k sample TTFT capture with streaming enabled and the customer's 32-token median client mix and share traces?

[27:12] Priya: yes will do, aim to share by Friday (2026-05-22).

[27:20] Jordan: Mike — can you add the client logs and run with the SDK streaming sample in a dev environment and share results next week?

[27:30] Mike: yep we'll run and send logs by Sun 24th.

[27:50] [29:00] Jordan: billing/pricing — I'll follow-up with Dedicated pool pricing. Also we'll include recommended reserved commit sizes that give the throughput you need.

[29:25] Jordan: any other questions on the data or traces?

[29:33] David: one ask — can Priya annotate traces with kernel and memcpy breakdown per-request? that would help our perf team.

[29:40] Priya: yes will annotate and upload.

[30:00] [31:00] Tom: timeline for deeper kernel/quant session?

[31:08] Jordan: propose 2026-05-27 for a technical deep-dive with SREs and SEs — agree?

[31:15] Mike: works for us.

[31:20] Priya: we'll cover driver matrix, fused kernel options, quant profiles, and examples of prefix caching patterns.

[31:40] Anita: I'll bring node tracing examples and recommended isolation configs.

[32:00] [33:00] Priya: quick recap of tuning knobs discussed:
- enable streaming for critical routes
- use prefix caching for static system prompts (with TTL and KMS)
- kernel override to fused attention for short seqs on dedicated
- small batching windows (4-6ms) or per-route batching policies
- session pooling when permitted

[33:40] Jordan: final notes — we'll send the cost/commit modeling and Detailed traces. Next meeting — the weekly POC sync on 2026-05-26 same time.

[34:10] Mike: thanks everyone — appreciate the clear action items.

[34:20] [35:00] Hannah: one last security ask — can you provide SOC2 scope for prefix caching and KMS integration?

[35:10] Sam: yes we'll attach the SOC2 appendix and KMS integration docs in the email.

[35:30] Jordan: great. thanks all. meeting end.

(End of transcript)
